'''''Erigeron strigosus''''' is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Asteraceae]] known by the common names '''prairie fleabane''',<ref name=plantsdb>{{Cite PLANTS
| date        = 2014
| id          = ERST3
| taxon       = Erigeron strigosus
| access-date = 29 September 2021
}}</ref> '''common eastern fleabane''',<ref name=fna>{{eFloras
| 1
| 242416508
| Erigeron strigosus
| volume      = 20
| tribe       = Astereae
| last1       = Nesom | first1 = G.L.   | author-link1 = Guy L. Nesom
| access-date = 29 September 2021
}}</ref> and '''daisy fleabane'''.<ref name=ilwf>{{Illinois Wildflowers
| prairie/plantx/ds_fleabanex
| Daisy fleabane
| access-date = 29 September 2021
}}</ref>

''Erigeron strigosus'' is native to eastern and central North America as far west as [[Manitoba]], [[Idaho]] and [[Texas]]. It has also become naturalized in western [[North America]] as well as in [[Europe]] and [[China]] as a somewhat weedy [[introduced species|naturalized species]].<ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/State/Erigeron%20strigosus.png Biota of North America Program 2014 state-level distribution map].</ref><ref name=foc>{{eFloras
| 2
| 242416508
| Erigeron strigosus
| volume      = 20
| tribe       = Astereae
| last1       = Chen      | first1 = Y.
| last2       = Brouillet | first2 = L. | author-link2 = Luc Brouillet
| access-date = 29 September 2021
}}</ref><ref>[http://www.tela-botanica.org/bdtfx-nn-24954-synthese Tela Botanica, Asteraceae, ''Erigeron strigosus'' Mühl. ex Willd., Vergerette maigre] in French with French distribution map and other information.</ref>

''Erigeron strigosus'' is an annual or biennial herb reaching heights of up to 80 cm (32 inches). It has hairy, [[Petiole (botany)|petioled]], non-clasping, [[Leaf shape|oval-shaped leaves]] a few centimeters long mostly on the lower part of the plant. One plant can produce as many as 200 [[flower heads]] in a spindly array of branching stems. Each head is less than a centimeter (0.4 inches) wide, containing 50–100 white, pink, or blue [[ray florets]] surrounding numerous yellow [[disc floret]]s.<ref name=fna/>

;Varieties<ref name=fna/>
*''Erigeron strigosus'' var. ''calcicola'' J. R. Allison - [[Alabama]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], [[Tennessee]]
*''Erigeron strigosus'' var. ''dolomiticola'' J. R. Allison - [[Alabama]]
*''Erigeron strigosus'' var. ''strigosus'' - much of North America; introduced in China
*''Erigeron strigosus'' var. ''septentrionalis'' (Fernald & Wiegand) Fernald - much of North America; introduced in Europe

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Erigeron strigosus'' var. ''calcicola'' is found in the central basin of [[Tennessee]], northwest [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]], northern [[Alabama]], and southwest/central [[Kentucky]]. It grows in limestone glades.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Erigeron allisonii (Cedar Glade Daisy Fleabane) - FSUS |url=https://fsus.ncbg.unc.edu/main.php?pg=show-taxon-detail.php&taxonid=5973 |access-date=2025-08-27 |website=fsus.ncbg.unc.edu |language=en}}</ref>

''Erigeron strigosus'' var. ''dolomiticola'' is endemic to [[Bibb County, Alabama|Bibb County]], Alabama, and grows in [[calcareous glade]]s.

''E. strigosus var. strigosus'' is distributed widely in North America and is found in disturbed areas, such as along roadsides, and open woodlands.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Erigeron strigosus var. strigosus (Common Rough Fleabane) - FSUS |url=https://fsus.ncbg.unc.edu/main.php?pg=show-taxon.php&&plantname=Erigeron+strigosus&limit=1&offset=2&taxonid=5974 |access-date=2025-08-27 |website=fsus.ncbg.unc.edu |language=en}}</ref>

''E. strigosus'' var. ''septentrionalis'' is also found throughout much of North America and grows on roadsides and in other disturbed areas.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Erigeron strigosus var. septentrionalis - FSUS |url=https://fsus.ncbg.unc.edu/main.php?pg=show-taxon.php&&plantname=Erigeron+strigosus&limit=1&offset=1&taxonid=5979 |access-date=2025-08-27 |website=fsus.ncbg.unc.edu |language=en}}</ref>

== Pollen ==
''Erigeron strigosus'' reproduces asexually and sexually in the southeastern United States.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Geographic parthenogenesis: A case study of sexual and apomictic Erigeron strigosus Muhl. ex Willd. (prairie fleabane) in the southeastern United States - ProQuest |url=https://www.proquest.com/openview/386e528f1285b541cd4f71353d4fe84d/1?pq-origsite=gscholar&cbl=18750&diss=y |access-date=2025-02-14 |website=www.proquest.com |language=en}}</ref> Pollen of ''Erigeron strigosus'' has been studied, larger higher quality pollen grains are typically sexual and smaller lower quality pollen grains are apomictic. Large pollen grains of ''Erigeron strigosus'' have more variable size which implies more sexual than asexual reproduction.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Noyes |first1=Richard D. |last2=Givens |first2=Amy D. |date=November 2013 |title=Quantitative Assessment of Megasporogenesis for the Facultative Apomicts Erigeron annuus and Erigeron strigosus (Asteraceae) |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/673243?journalCode=ijps |journal=International Journal of Plant Sciences |volume=174 |issue=9 |pages=1239–1250 |doi=10.1086/673243 |issn=1058-5893|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Invasive ==
This species is native to eastern and central North America but has become invasive in parts of Asia and Europe. ''Erigeron strigosus'' was falsely identified as ''E. annuus'' in China because as foreign species they were not well known.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Erigeron strigosus in Flora of China @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242416508 |access-date=2025-02-12 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref> It was also observed as a common invasive in Poland and forms hybrids with ''Erigeron'' ''annuus,'' two [[Karyotype|cytotypes]] of ''Erigeron strigosus'' were reported, a triploid (3''n''=27 and 4''n''=36) and hexaploid form.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pliszko |first1=Artur |last2=Łazarski |first2=Grzegorz |last3=Musiał |first3=Krystyna |last4=Kalinowski |first4=Paweł |date=2024 |title=New records on chromosome numbers in non-native "Erigeron" L. taxa (Asteraceae) from Poland |url=https://bazawiedzy.uksw.edu.pl/info/article/UKSW173d85a4ff8343129e3d1ff773ea96f8/ |journal=BioInvasions Records |language=en |volume=13 |issue=4 |pages=843–853 |doi=10.3391/bir.2024.13.4.01 |issn=2242-1300|doi-access=free }}</ref> It is able to easily adapt to new regions and cross with closely related species. The family and genus ''Erigeron'' was found to have high taxonomic diversity within Russia and Europe, novel hybrids, contributes to the invasiveness of the species.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sennikov |first1=Alexander N. |last2=Kozhin |first2=Mikhail N. |date=2023-11-15 |title=Taxonomic revision of the Erigeron acris group (Asteraceae) in Murmansk Region, Russia, reveals a complex pattern of native and alien taxa |journal=PhytoKeys |language=en |issue=235 |pages=83–128 |doi=10.3897/phytokeys.235.111020 |doi-access=free |issn=1314-2003 |pmc=10665865 |pmid=38020474}}</ref>

== Fire ecology ==
In part of its range ''Erigeron strigosus'' is found in tall grass prairie where fire is a regular part of the ecosystem. The cycle of fire initially causes a reduction of ''Erigeron strigosus,'' but it increases two to three years after fire.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gibson |first=David J. |date=1988 |title=Regeneration and Fluctuation of Tallgrass Prairie Vegetation in Rresponse to Burning Frequency |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2996561 |journal=Bulletin of the Torrey Botanical Club |volume=115 |issue=1 |pages=1–12 |doi=10.2307/2996561 |jstor=2996561 |issn=0040-9618|url-access=subscription }}</ref> It often germinates in response to fire disturbance, and its germination rates are higher with fire disturbance than without.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Abrams |first=Marc D. |date=1988-03-30 |title=Effects of Burning Regime on Buried Seed Banks and Canopy Coverage in a Kansas Tallgrass Prairie |url=https://doi.org/10.2307/3672089 |journal=The Southwestern Naturalist |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=65 |doi=10.2307/3672089 |issn=0038-4909|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The cycle of fire also reduces the incidence of infections on ''Erigeron strigosus'' such as rust fungus ''[[Puccinia dioicae]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dendy |first1=S. P. |last2=Tong |first2=B. |last3=Alexander |first3=H. M. |last4=Fay |first4=P. A. |last5=Murray |first5=L. |last6=Xing |first6=Y. |last7=Garrett |first7=K. A. |date=2017 |title=A long-term study of burning effects on a plant pathogen in tallgrass prairie |url=https://bsppjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ppa.12678 |journal=Plant Pathology |language=en |volume=66 |issue=8 |pages=1308–1317 |doi=10.1111/ppa.12678 |issn=1365-3059|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Overall, increasing fire frequency has a positive effect on ''E. strigosus.''<ref>{{Citation |last=Chapman |first=Julia I. |chapter=Topography and Vegetation Patterns in an Old-Growth Appalachian Forest: Lucy Braun, You Were Right! |date=2018 |title=Ecology and Recovery of Eastern Old-Growth Forests |pages=83–98 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.5822/978-1-61091-891-6_5 |access-date=2025-08-27 |place=Washington, DC |publisher=Island Press/Center for Resource Economics |isbn=978-1-61091-991-3 |last2=McEwan |first2=Ryan W.}}</ref>

==Ecology==

''Erigeron strigosus'' is insect pollinated and is recorded to have been visited in northern Florida by ''[[Agapostemon splendens]]'', ''[[Augochloropsis metallica]]'', and ''[[Ceratina]]'', ''Halictus poeyi/ligatus'', ''Heriades variolosa/leavitti'', ''Lasioglossum longifrons'', ''[[Lasioglossum pectorale]]'', ''[[Lasioglossum reticulatum]]'', ''[[Lasioglossum vierecki]]'', and ''[[Megachile petulans]]''.<ref>Ulyshen, M. D., K. Robertson, S. Horn, and C. Dixon. 2024. Characterization of the bee community and pollination network in a southeastern U.S. pine savanna. Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution 12:1403602.</ref>
